section.title: Paul's Gospel from God
section.sectionRationale: Having pronounced a curse on any rival gospel, Paul now defends where his gospel came from. It was not devised by man nor taught to him, but received by revelation from Jesus Christ. He tells his own story, from zealous persecutor to called apostle, and shows that he owed his message to God, not to Jerusalem, so that the churches even glorified God because of him.
section.thesis: Paul's gospel is authoritative because it came by revelation from Jesus Christ, not from human tradition; the same God who set him apart before birth and turned the persecutor into a preacher is the guarantee that the message of grace is God's own and cannot be improved by human addition.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the claim that the gospel came by revelation, not from man; Paul's former life in Judaism and God's gracious call to reveal His Son in him; and Paul's limited early contact with Jerusalem, proving his independence, with the churches glorifying God.

units.label: Not devised by man
units.note: received by revelation from Jesus Christ

verses.text: For I want you to know, brothers, that the gospel I preached was not devised by man.
I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it; rather, I received it by {{apokalypsis|revelation}} from Jesus Christ.

units.label: From persecutor to called
units.note: God set him apart and called him by grace

verses.text: For you have heard of my former way of life in {{ioudaismos|Judaism}}, how severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it.
I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries and was extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers.
But when God, who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by His {{charis|grace}}, was pleased
to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles, I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood,
nor did I go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who came before me, but I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus.

units.label: Little contact with Jerusalem
units.note: unknown by face, they glorified God

verses.text: Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days.
But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord's brother.
I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie.
Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
I was personally unknown, however, to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.
They only heard the account: “The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.”
And they glorified God because of me.

apokalypsis.gloss: A revelation, an unveiling, a disclosure of what was hidden. Paul insists his gospel came by apokalypsis from Jesus Christ, not by human instruction. The word points back to the Damascus road, where the risen Christ made Himself known and commissioned Paul directly, so the message carries divine, not merely human, authority.

ioudaismos.gloss: Judaism, the whole way of life ordered by the law and the traditions of the fathers. Paul had excelled in it and was violently zealous for it, which makes his conversion all the more striking. Only God's intervention could turn so committed a defender of the traditions into a preacher of grace to the Gentiles.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's unearned favor. Paul says God called him by His grace, verse 15, while he was still a persecutor of the church. Grace, not merit, explains both his salvation and his commission; the man who tried to destroy the church became its apostle purely by God's free favor.

basic.context: Paul keeps defending the gospel by defending where it came from. His opponents may have said his message was second hand, learned from the Jerusalem apostles and then softened. Paul answers with his own story: he received the gospel directly from the risen Christ. He was a fierce persecutor, God called him by grace, and only later did he have brief contact with Jerusalem, so his gospel is God's, not man's.
basic.hermeneutics: This is autobiography with a purpose. Every detail, the persecuting past, the direct call, the years away, the short visits, serves one point: Paul's gospel was not handed down by human teachers and cannot be edited by them. Read it as Paul's evidence that grace is God's own message.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul says he received the gospel by apokalypsis, revelation, an unveiling by the risen Christ. He describes his former life in ioudaismos, Judaism, where he was violently zealous. And he traces everything to charis, grace, for God called him while he was still a persecutor.
basic.typology: God setting Paul apart from his mother's womb echoes the calling of the prophets, Jeremiah and the servant of Isaiah, chosen before birth for God's purposes. Paul's turnaround pictures the gospel he preaches: the enemy of God is reconciled by grace and made a herald of the very faith he opposed.
basic.christ: The center of the passage is that God was pleased to reveal His Son in Paul. Christ is the content of the gospel and the one who commissions Paul directly. The risen Jesus is the source of Paul's message, which is why no human authority can override it.
basic.god: God set Paul apart before birth, called him by grace, and was pleased to reveal His Son in him. God takes the initiative at every step, choosing, calling, and revealing. The result is that God gets the glory: the Judean churches glorified God because of what He had done in Paul.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 9 tells of Paul's conversion on the Damascus road. Jeremiah 1 speaks of being set apart before birth. Philippians 3 lists Paul's credentials in Judaism, now counted as loss for Christ.
basic.oneStory: God delights to make enemies into worshipers. Paul the persecutor becomes Paul the apostle, a living sample of the grace he preaches. The story runs on the same grace that will save the Galatians, the grace the false teachers are in danger of trading away.

context.literary:
Here the letter changes from rebuke to narrative, and the narrative is built as evidence. Paul does not tell his story for its own sake. Every clause is placed to answer one question: did anyone give him this gospel? The section opens with the thesis in verses 11 and 12, a double denial and a single claim, and then spends twelve verses showing the claim was true by the way the facts fall out.

The narrative runs in three blocks that are marked by their contrast with Jerusalem. Verses 13 and 14 describe the man he was, and the Greek is built from a series of imperfect verbs that make the persecution and the advance continuous. Verses 15 and 16 give the turning point in one long sentence, a single subordinate chain with God as the subject and Paul only the object, until the main verb at the end of verse 16, 'I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood.' Verses 17 to 24 then trace his movements by a string of negatives and of small timekeeping words: 'nor did I go up,' 'only after three years,' 'later,' 'I saw none of the other apostles except James.'

The geography is itself an argument. Paul goes to Arabia, back to Damascus, then to Jerusalem for fifteen days, and then to Syria and Cilicia. At no point does he stay long enough in Jerusalem to be taught. The oath of verse 20, 'I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie,' sits at the exact midpoint of the itinerary, where the claim is most likely to be doubted.

The passage ends with the voice of other churches. The report in verse 23 is given in direct speech, and it is the evidence of strangers: 'The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.' The last clause turns the whole account into a doxology: 'And they glorified God because of me.'
context.historical:
The chronology of Paul's first years as a Christian is compressed here, and putting it together with Acts takes care. He was raised in Tarsus, trained in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, Acts 22:3, and became the leading enforcer against the new movement. Luke has him consenting to Stephen's death, Acts 8:1, and travelling to Damascus with letters from the high priest, Acts 9:1-2. Paul's own language in verse 13 matches: he persecuted 'severely' and tried to 'destroy' the church.

After the vision on the Damascus road, Acts says he spent days with the disciples there and began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, Acts 9:19-22. Galatians adds a detail Acts does not give, the journey into Arabia. In his day, Arabia meant the Nabatean kingdom to the south and east of Damascus. Paul does not say what he did there, and whether it was a time of preaching, of reflection or both is not recorded. When Paul came back to Damascus, the city was under the control of a governor of King Aretas, who tried to arrest him, 2 Corinthians 11:32-33. The escape in a basket through a window in the wall fits Acts 9:23-25.

The three years of verse 18 are most likely counted from his conversion. At that point he goes to Jerusalem to meet Cephas, which is Peter's Aramaic name, and stays fifteen days. Acts 9:26-30 gives the other side: the disciples there were afraid of him until Barnabas took him to the apostles. Paul stresses that he saw only Peter and James, 'the Lord's brother.' The reference to James here is important, since James later leads the Jerusalem church and his name will return in 2:9 and 2:12.

The churches of Judea knew him only by report, and Syria and Cilicia were the regions around Antioch and his native Tarsus. The years there are the years before Barnabas fetched him for Antioch, Acts 11:25-26.
context.canonical:
The language of verse 15 echoes the calling of the prophets. Jeremiah heard God say, 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations,' Jeremiah 1:5. The Servant of Isaiah says, 'The LORD called Me from the womb,' and is told that it is not enough to raise up Jacob, for He will be a light to the nations, Isaiah 49:1-6. Paul does not quote either, but the shape of the sentence leans on both: set apart before birth, called, and sent to the nations. By using that pattern, he places his own call inside the line of those who were sent by God before they knew it.

The story is told three times in Acts, and in each a different aspect is highlighted. Acts 9 gives the vision and the early days in Damascus. In Acts 22 Paul tells the crowd in Jerusalem of the voice of the Lord and the instruction to go to the Gentiles, Acts 22:17-21. In Acts 26 he reports Christ's words, 'I am sending you to them to open their eyes,' Acts 26:16-18. Galatians gives the version aimed at a church that was being told he was a second hand apostle.

Paul returns to his history in other letters. To the Philippians he lists the credentials he had counted as gain, Philippians 3:4-6, and he calls himself the least of the apostles because he persecuted the church of God, 1 Corinthians 15:9-10. To Timothy he calls himself the worst of sinners and sees his mercy as an example, 1 Timothy 1:13-16. In each he lets the reader see that the grace he preaches was first spent on him.

Jesus' words to Peter set a pattern: 'this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven,' Matthew 16:17. Paul uses the same words, 'flesh and blood', for the human sources that did not teach him.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the Galatians to be able to answer one question for themselves: where does the gospel come from? The rival teachers had a strong claim. They represented Jerusalem, they were with the first disciples, and by implication the Galatians had received a secondhand version from a junior figure who had never sat with Jesus. If Paul's gospel was only a human tradition, then those who held the older and more official version could correct it. Paul's story shuts that door. It shows a message that reached him before any human authority had a chance to shape it.

He also meant the story to be a demonstration of grace. By telling them how fierce a persecutor he had been, he sets the stage for the phrase 'called me by His grace.' A man who was breathing out threats could not have earned the gospel by prior religious merit, since his religious record was exactly what made him an enemy. The Galatians were tempted to think that religious achievement could secure standing with God. Paul's own life is a counterexample.

A third purpose is protective. He wants them to hear that he does not despise the Jerusalem apostles. He went up to see Peter, and he acknowledges James. The point is not that he is better than they are but that his message was given independently and later confirmed by them, as the next chapter will show. He is not setting himself against the church but standing with it on the ground God gave him.

Finally he invites them to join the glorifying of God. The Judean churches heard the report and praised God. The Galatians, who have also heard, should do the same, and not turn away from the gospel that had so changed their teacher.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage is autobiography. It records what happened to Paul and where he went, and it should not be read as a command that every believer must have a Damascus road experience or spend three years in the desert. Paul's call was unique, because he was an apostle commissioned directly by the risen Lord, and the 'revelation' of verse 12 is the ground of apostolic authority, not a template for ordinary Christian experience.

What the passage prescribes is more subtle. It teaches that the gospel is not shaped by human committees, and that the message the church holds is a received message, not an invented one. It also teaches that grace works on people who look beyond reach. Anyone who thinks that a person's past rules out their future should read verses 13 to 16 again.

It is worth noting what is not said. Paul does not claim that he never learned from anyone. He uses Scripture and the church's teaching elsewhere, and 1 Corinthians 15:3 says he 'received' and 'passed on' the core of the message. The point of Galatians 1 is not that no human being ever spoke to him about Jesus but that the gospel's content and authority came from Christ himself, and no one added to it.

debates.question: What does 'to reveal His Son in me' mean?

views.label: Revealed inwardly, in Paul's heart
views.case: The Greek preposition is the ordinary word for 'in,' and verse 12 had spoken of a revelation of Jesus Christ to him. Paul elsewhere says Christ lives in him, Galatians 2:20, and this reading takes the revelation as an inward unveiling that made him a preacher.

views.label: Revealed to Paul, as the recipient
views.case: The same preposition can mean 'to' or 'by means of,' and the other accounts of the Damascus road, Acts 9:3-5 and Acts 26:16, describe an event Paul saw and heard. On this view the phrase says that the Son was made known to him.

views.label: Revealed through Paul, as the means
views.case: A third view takes the phrase to mean that God revealed His Son in and through Paul's life and preaching, so that the Gentiles could see Christ in the messenger. Verse 24, where the churches glorify God 'because of me,' uses the same preposition and fits this.

debates.bearing: These are not mutually exclusive. The key point is the same in all three: the initiative lay with God, and the content was the Son. Paul's life became both the place where Christ was seen and the means by which others would see Him.

debates.question: Was Paul converted from one religion to another or called within the faith of Israel?

views.label: A conversion from Judaism to Christianity
views.case: Paul speaks of his 'former way of life in Judaism,' which implies something has been left behind, and he describes himself as having been a persecutor of the church of God. Philippians 3:7-8 calls his old gains loss for Christ.

views.label: A call within the faith of Israel
views.case: Some stress that Paul never speaks of leaving the God of Israel, and that the language of 'called' and 'set apart' resembles that of the prophets. On this view he did not change gods but recognised the Messiah his own Scriptures had promised.

debates.bearing: Paul's own words hold both. He turned away from a zeal that persecuted, and he did so as an Israelite who now saw the promises fulfilled. The point for Galatians is that the way of life he left behind could not make anyone right with God.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 11 uses gnorizo, 'I make known,' a verb Paul uses when he wants to bring something to the readers' attention for emphasis. It is an announcement, and it opens a statement about the gospel's origin: it is not 'according to man,' kata anthropon. The preposition kata with the accusative means conformed to a human pattern. Paul is saying the gospel does not follow human standards of what a message from God ought to be, an idea he develops in 1 Corinthians 1:23-25.

In verse 12 he sets two verbs side by side, parelabon, 'I received,' and edidachthen, 'I was taught.' The first is the standard word for taking over a tradition from someone who handed it down, as in 1 Corinthians 15:3. The second is the word for being instructed by a teacher. He denies both. He then adds apokalypsis, 'revelation,' an unveiling. The phrase 'of Jesus Christ' that follows is in the genitive, and that can mean Jesus Christ was the one who unveiled, or the one who was unveiled. Paul may well mean both, as the idea fits Acts 26:16.

In verses 13 and 14 the noun ioudaismos is used for Paul's former way of life. It names a way of life as well as a religion and appears in the New Testament only here, in these two verses. His persecution is described with two verbs in the imperfect tense, 'I was persecuting' and 'I was ravaging,' the second of which, eporthoun, carries the sense of laying waste, and the phrase kath' hyperbolen means 'to an extreme degree.' The continuing tense draws a picture of sustained effort, not a single act. He was a zealot, zelotes, for the traditions handed down, paradoseis, a word that matches his later use of 'received' for the gospel.

In verse 15 the verb translated 'set apart' is aphorizo, and Paul uses its participle of himself in Romans 1:1, 'set apart for the gospel of God.' It is the language of separation to a task. In verse 16 he says he did not 'consult with flesh and blood,' using prosanatithemai, a verb for referring a matter to someone for advice or interpretation. The phrase 'flesh and blood' is the same idiom Jesus used to Peter in Matthew 16:17.

In verse 18 the verb for visiting Cephas is historesai, which means to inquire, to get acquainted with, and gives us the English word history. The meaning is that Paul went to get to know Peter, not to be taught by him. Verse 22 calls himself 'unknown,' agnooumenos, to the churches of Judea. 'By face,' to prosopo, the idiom is literal: they had not seen his face, but only heard the report.

typology.type: The prophet set apart before birth, Jeremiah 1:5
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah was known and set apart before he was formed, and appointed to the nations. Paul's language about being set apart from his mother's womb claims the same line. The correspondence is the call before any merit and the mission to the nations. In Christ it escalates, for Paul is sent not under the old covenant to warn, but in the new to proclaim a finished work, 2 Corinthians 5:19-20. The type falls short because Jeremiah's mission was mostly of judgment and uprooting, while Paul is sent with good news.

typology.type: The Servant who becomes a light to the nations, Isaiah 49:1-6
typology.fulfillment: The Servant says the LORD called Him from the womb, and is told that raising up Jacob is too small a task, for He will be a light to the nations. Jesus is that Servant, and Paul's call echoes it because he carries the light to the Gentiles in His name, Acts 13:47. The correspondence is the prenatal call and the widening to the nations. Paul is a servant of the Servant, and the type falls short in that only Christ brings salvation, while Paul is a witness to it.

The enemy of God's people who becomes their champion has parallels in Israel's story, where God turns hearts, as with Joseph's brothers. In Paul it becomes a public pattern. He says in 1 Timothy 1:16 that Christ displayed His perfect patience in him as an example to those who would believe. The escalation is that the mercy goes beyond the forgiveness of an enemy to the making of an apostle. The type falls short in that Paul is not the saviour but a sample of what grace does.

study.christ:
Christ stands at both ends of the passage. In verse 12 He is the source of the gospel: Paul received it by revelation 'from Jesus Christ.' In verse 16 He is its content, the Son whom God was pleased to reveal. The apostolic message is not a set of ideas that Christ taught and that someone then wrote down. It is the person of the risen Lord making Himself known. For Paul, that was the moment on the Damascus road, where the voice said, 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,' Acts 9:5.

That answer carries a lesson about the church. The Lord says that to persecute the disciples is to persecute Him. This is why the persecutor has to be struck at the root of his zeal. Paul had thought he was serving God by defending the law, and discovered that he was fighting the one the law was about. The risen Christ identifies Himself with His people, and that unity of the Lord with the church is one of the engines of the New Testament, from the Gospel of Matthew, 'whatever you did for one of the least of these,' to Paul's phrase 'the body of Christ.'

The passage also shows Christ as the one who commissions. Paul's apostleship came from Christ, as the first verse of the letter said. The Gentile mission is by His command, 'so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles.' The aim of the mission is the preaching of the Son, not the preaching of a system. The gospel Paul brings is a person.

There is a pattern of grace here, too. The Son came to save sinners, and Paul counts himself the foremost, 1 Timothy 1:15. In his own life the saving mercy of Christ meets him when he is least deserving. That is the same grace in the greeting, 'the grace of Christ,' 1:6, by which the Galatians were called. The story of Paul is a case study in what the cross accomplished.

None of this requires reading Paul as a type of Christ. He is not one. He is the recipient and the herald. What the passage does show is that the gospel is Christ-given and Christ-centred, so that no teacher can improve on it.
study.god:
The first and strongest point is that God takes the initiative. Verse 15 is built so that God is the subject of nearly everything: He set Paul apart, He called, He was pleased to reveal His Son. Paul's own actions come only after, and only in negative form: he did not consult, he did not go up. This is the reverse of how the false teachers saw salvation, as a human achievement. In Paul's account the human part is response.

God is shown as having a plan that goes before the person. 'From my mother's womb' says that the purpose existed before Paul could do anything, good or bad. It does not say God made him a persecutor, but that the persecution could not frustrate what God had set in motion. The same truth comes in Ephesians 1:4, where He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world. This is a God whose purposes are wider than our history.

God is also gracious in a way that scandalises. A man who destroyed the church is not only forgiven but made a preacher of the faith he tried to destroy. Verse 15 gives the reason in two words: 'by His grace.' Not because of repentance that preceded it, not because of promise in his character, and not because of religious sincerity, but by grace. This is what Paul means in 1 Corinthians 15:10, 'by the grace of God I am what I am.'

The passage shows that God is pleased to do this. The verb of verse 15, 'was pleased,' speaks of His delight and goodwill. The call of Paul was not an unwilling concession. It reveals a God who finds joy in making enemies into worshippers.

Finally, God receives the glory. In verse 24 the Judean churches glorified God, because of what He had done in the man who had been their persecutor. The proper response to a story of grace is praise to the giver, not admiration for the one who received it. This also teaches worship. The church today honours God best when it tells how He has done the unexpected in a life, and gives Him the credit.

crossReferences.note: Luke's account of the Damascus road gives the other side of the story: the persecuting journey, the light, and the voice that says 'Why do you persecute Me?' It confirms Galatians 1:13 and 1:16 and supplies the detail that the Lord identifies Himself with His people.

Paul tells the Jerusalem crowd of his education under Gamaliel and his zeal against the Way. It supports the picture of Galatians 1:14, where he advanced beyond his contemporaries in zeal for the traditions of his fathers.

Christ's commission to Paul includes the words 'I am sending you to them to open their eyes.' It shows that the call to the Gentiles was from the beginning, matching the purpose clause of Galatians 1:16.
The prophet's call came before his birth and reached to the nations. Paul's wording in verse 15 leans on this call, placing himself in the line of messengers who were sent before they knew it.

The Servant is called from the womb and made a light to the nations. The pattern of a call before birth joined to a mission for the Gentiles is the closest Old Testament match to Paul's own description.

Paul's list of credentials, circumcised, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, faultless as to righteousness in the law, and as to zeal, persecuting the church. It fills in the former life that Galatians 1:13-14 summarises.

Paul calls himself a blasphemer, a persecutor and a violent man who was shown mercy, and sees his own case as an example of Christ's perfect patience. It turns the story told in Galatians 1 into a pattern for other believers.

Jesus tells Peter that this was not revealed by flesh and blood but by His Father. Paul's refusal to consult flesh and blood in Galatians 1:16 uses the same phrase, and sets his knowledge of Christ beside Peter's as a gift from God.
Paul calls himself the least of the apostles because he persecuted the church of God, yet says by God's grace he is what he is. It is a short echo of the whole story of Galatians 1:13-24.
After Damascus, Saul came to Jerusalem and the disciples were afraid of him until Barnabas took him to the apostles. This is the Jerusalem visit of Galatians 1:18, told from the church's side.
Paul tells of the governor under King Aretas who sought to arrest him in Damascus and of his escape in a basket. It fills in the political setting of the return to Damascus in Galatians 1:17.
Paul introduces himself as set apart for the gospel of God, which concerns His Son. The same verb for set apart appears here and in Galatians 1:15, and the same Son is at the centre.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's central problem is that humanity, made to know God, turned away and became His enemy. The story of rescue is the story of God going after His enemies. Galatians 1:13-24 gives one case in miniature. Paul is not simply a wayward believer. He is an active opponent, using religious zeal to attack the people of God, and God finds him.

Looking back, the passage answers a theme that runs from Genesis onward: God's choice of unlikely people. He called Abraham out of a family that served other gods, took Moses from the wilderness after a murder, and made David the king over the whole nation from among the shepherds. Paul's story belongs on that list. The calling of the prophets before birth, as in Jeremiah, adds that the choice was made before any record of obedience.

Looking forward, the passage prepares for the central argument of Galatians. If God calls by grace and not by merit, then the Galatians cannot add anything of their own to be accepted. Chapter 2 will show the leaders in Jerusalem recognising the same grace in Paul, and chapter 3 will root that grace in the promise to Abraham that came before the law. The question of what Paul brought to his own salvation is the question the Galatians must ask about theirs.

The story also touches the mission of God to the nations. God told Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and Paul is the one commissioned to preach Christ among the Gentiles. In him the old promise about the nations meets its working out. The Judean churches, who had been persecuted, hear the news and glorify God, which is a small picture of the reconciliation God is forming.

Finally, the end of the story is in sight. The vision of a great multitude from every nation worshipping God is where this mission is headed, Revelation 7:9. Every person turned from enmity to praise, as Paul was, brings that day nearer.

sermon.title: No Human Invention (Galatians 1:11 to 24)
sermon.why: Begg expounds Paul's insistence that the gospel was not a human invention but a revelation from Jesus Christ, tracing Paul's conversion and independence to show that the message of grace carries God's own authority.

quiz.q: Where does Paul say his gospel came from?

options.text: By revelation from Jesus Christ, not from any man.
options.note: Verse 12 grounds the gospel in direct revelation from Christ.

options.text: From careful study of the traditions of his fathers.
options.note: Those traditions marked his old life; the gospel came by revelation, not tradition.

options.text: From the apostles who trained him in Jerusalem.
options.note: Paul stresses he did not receive it from the Jerusalem apostles.

options.text: From his own clever reasoning.
options.note: He denies it was devised by man at all.

quiz.q: What was Paul's life like before God called him?

options.text: He violently persecuted the church and was zealous for the traditions.
options.note: Verses 13 and 14 describe his fierce opposition to the church.

options.text: He was already a quiet follower of Jesus.
options.note: The opposite; he tried to destroy the church.

options.text: He was indifferent to religion altogether.
options.note: He was extremely zealous, not indifferent.

options.text: He was a Gentile with no interest in the law.
options.note: He advanced in Judaism beyond his contemporaries.

quiz.q: Why does Paul stress his limited early contact with Jerusalem?

options.text: To show his gospel came from God directly, not second hand from other men.
options.note: The timeline proves the independence of his message.

options.text: To prove he disagreed with all the other apostles.
options.note: He shows independence of source, not a different gospel.

options.text: To boast that he never needed other believers.
options.note: The point is the origin of his gospel, not self sufficiency.

options.text: Because he was ashamed of the Jerusalem church.
options.note: He honors the church; the churches glorified God because of him.

options.text: God set him apart and called him by grace.
options.note: Verse 15 credits grace, not merit, for his calling.

options.text: His own decision to become more religious.
options.note: He was already intensely religious; the change came from God's grace.

options.text: Pressure from the Jerusalem apostles.
options.note: The call came from God directly, not from apostolic pressure.

options.text: A gradual change of mind over many years.
options.note: God's gracious call and revelation of His Son were the cause.

quiz.q: How did the Judean churches respond to news about Paul?

options.text: They glorified God because the persecutor was now preaching the faith.
options.note: Verse 24 shows God got the glory for the change in Paul.

options.text: They refused to believe he had really changed.
options.note: They heard the account and glorified God, rather than rejecting it.

options.text: They resented that he was preaching without their permission.
options.note: The text records worship, not resentment.

options.text: They ignored the news entirely.
options.note: They actively glorified God because of him.

questions: Paul's gospel came by revelation, not human invention. How does it change your confidence to know the gospel is God's message and not a human theory?
Paul was a zealous, religious man who was still opposed to God. Where might sincere religious effort actually be keeping someone from grace?
God called Paul while he was still a persecutor. Does anyone seem beyond the reach of grace to you, and how does Paul's story challenge that?
The churches glorified God because of the change in Paul. When people look at your life, what do they end up giving God credit for?
Paul refused to let anyone edit the gospel he received. What pressures tempt you to soften or add to the message of grace today?

translationNotes.note: Revelation translates apokalypsis, an unveiling; Paul points to the risen Christ making Himself known on the Damascus road as the source of his gospel.
Reveal His Son in me can also be rendered reveal His Son to me and through me; either way the emphasis is on God's direct disclosure of Christ.
Cephas is the Aramaic name for Peter, as the BSB footnote indicates; the two names refer to the same apostle.
